explanations.answer: Search for a young woman to care for him
explanations.explanation: That's the plan, baker. The servants say, “Let us search for a young virgin for our lord the king, to attend to him and care for him…” They aren't fiddling with the room or the furniture. They're looking for a person to look after David.

explanations.answer: Move him to a warmer room in the palace
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, because that's what most of us would try first. But the text never mentions a room change. The servants suggest a search for a young woman to attend to the king, and they go looking for her all over Israel. I once lived in a junk drawer, and trust me, a room doesn't care for you the way a person does.

explanations.answer: Keep a fire burning beside his bed
explanations.explanation: A fire makes sense, and I'm a cookie stamper who lives next to ovens, so I'm biased. But no fire shows up in this passage. The servants' plan is to find a young woman to care for the king and lie by his side to keep him warm. They already tried blankets, and the plan after that is a person.

explanations.answer: Chariots and fifty men to run ahead
explanations.explanation: Yep. Adonijah, one of David's sons, acquires “…chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him.” That's a whole parade. And he's saying “I will be king!” at the time.

explanations.answer: A crown and a robe of purple
explanations.explanation: That would be a fine outfit, baker, but the text doesn't mention either one. Adonijah, one of David's sons, gets chariots, horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him. He's showing off with a whole lineup, and a crown and a purple robe aren't in it.

explanations.answer: A palace guard of a hundred men
explanations.explanation: Close on the idea, but the number is off. The text says Adonijah, one of David's sons, gets fifty men to run ahead of him, along with chariots and horsemen. No palace guard is mentioned. Fifty runners out front is already plenty of attention.
It's the other way around, friend. The text says “His father had never once reprimanded him…” So David never once asked Adonijah why he acts this way. That's the one question David didn't ask.
Right on. The text says “His father had never once reprimanded him…” David never once asked Adonijah why he acts this way. And in that same stretch, Adonijah is saying “I will be king!”

Not this time, baker. Joab and Abiathar the priest are the ones who support Adonijah. Nathan the prophet is on the list of men who “…would not join Adonijah.” He isn't on Adonijah's side, and he's about to get involved.

That's the one. Adonijah confers with Joab and Abiathar the priest, who support him. But Nathan the prophet is named among those who “…would not join Adonijah.” Nathan isn't on his side, and we're about to see what he does next.

That's him. Solomon, another son of David, is the one left off. The text says Adonijah invited his royal brothers but “…did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon.” Whatever the reason, I think the empty chair is the loudest thing at that party.

Shephatiah does show up in the list of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:4), but he's not who this passage names. The text says Adonijah did not invite “…his brother Solomon.” So the one left out here is Solomon.

Chileab is one of David's sons in the family list (2 Samuel 3:3), so I see why he came to mind. But he's not the one this passage talks about. The text says Adonijah did not invite “…his brother Solomon.” and that's the name to remember.
Yes, and it's serious. Nathan, the prophet, tells Bathsheba, “Save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.” The stakes here are lives, not property.
A room is nice to keep, but it's not what Nathan says. He tells Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, to “Save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.” This is about her life and her son's life.

Land does matter to people, baker, but Nathan doesn't bring it up. He tells Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, “Save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.” He's talking about her life and Solomon's, not property.

Yep. Nathan tells Bathsheba to go to King David and remind him that he swore her son Solomon would reign after him and sit on his throne. Then she's to ask, “Why then has Adonijah become king?” It's a reminder with a question attached.

It's actually true, friend. Nathan tells Bathsheba to go at once to King David and remind him of what he swore. David swore that her son Solomon would reign after him and sit on his throne. Then she's to ask why Adonijah has become king.
That's the word. Nathan says, “…I will come in after you and confirm your words.” He's not going to argue with her or change her story. He plans to back her up.

Nathan does ask David a question once he's in the room, but that's not the word in his plan. He says he'll come in after Bathsheba and “…confirm your words.” His job there is to back her up, not cross-examine her.
Softening would be a gentle plan, friend, but Nathan doesn't say it. He tells Bathsheba, “…I will come in after you and confirm your words.” He plans to confirm what she says, not water it down.

That's right. Bathsheba tells David, “…the eyes of all Israel are upon you to tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.” She says the whole nation is waiting on his answer. That's a lot of eyes on one old king.

It's true, baker. Bathsheba says, “…the eyes of all Israel are upon you to tell them who will sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.” She's telling David that all Israel is waiting for him to name the next king.

explanations.answer: They will be counted as criminals
explanations.explanation: That's what she says. Bathsheba tells David that when he rests with his fathers, “…I and my son Solomon will be counted as criminals.” She's saying plainly what's at stake if David stays silent.

explanations.answer: They will be sent out of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Being sent away would be hard enough, but Bathsheba doesn't say it. She tells David that when he rests with his fathers, she and Solomon “…will be counted as criminals.” That's the danger she names.

explanations.answer: They will lose everything they own
explanations.explanation: Losing everything sounds like a believable worry, friend, but it's not what she says. Bathsheba tells David, “…I and my son Solomon will be counted as criminals.” That's the outcome she names.

explanations.answer: Did you say Adonijah will reign after you
explanations.explanation: That's how he opens. Nathan the prophet asks, “did you say, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne’?” He puts it to David as a question. Then he goes on to tell David what Adonijah has done.

explanations.answer: Did you hear the noise from En-rogel
explanations.explanation: En-rogel is where Adonijah's feast is, so I see the connection. But Nathan's question isn't about noise. He asks David, “did you say, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne’?” The loud noise comes later, from a different place.

explanations.answer: Did you send Joab to the sacrifice
explanations.explanation: Joab is at the feast, and Nathan does mention the army commanders being there. But that's not the question he asks. Nathan asks David, “did you say, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne’?”
That's what Nathan says they're saying. They are eating and drinking before Adonijah and saying, “Long live King Adonijah!” That's a whole party cheering for Adonijah as king.
They're not toasting David, friend. Nathan tells the king that Adonijah's guests are eating and drinking before Adonijah and saying, “Long live King Adonijah!” David is the one who hasn't been told.
That's close in spirit, but it's not the line. Nathan says the guests are saying, “Long live King Adonijah!” They're not calling him commander. They're calling him king.

Yep. Nathan tells David that Adonijah has not invited “me your servant… nor Zadok the priest, nor Benaiah son of Jehoiada, nor your servant Solomon.” Zadok is a priest, and he's on the list of people left out. Nathan names himself on that list too.
Zadok is on that list, baker. Nathan tells David that Adonijah has not invited him, “…nor Zadok the priest, nor Benaiah son of Jehoiada, nor your servant Solomon.” Zadok the priest was left out too.
That's the word. David swears, “I will carry out this very day exactly what I swore to you…” That's no maybe-later. The king says it happens the same day.
I get why "someday" sounds like a king's answer, baker, but David doesn't leave it there. He swears, “I will carry out this very day exactly what I swore to you…” He says this very day.
Next year would have been a long wait with Adonijah's feast going on right now. David doesn't say that. He swears, “I will carry out this very day exactly what I swore to you…”

That's right. David says, “Set my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon.” Riding the king's own mule is a loud way to show who's picked. It's David's mule, not a chariot like the ones Adonijah acquired.
Adonijah is the one with the chariots, friend. When David gives the order, he says, “Set my son Solomon on my own mule…” It's David's mule, not a chariot.
A war horse would look impressive, but that's not what David orders. He says, “Set my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon.” Solomon rides the king's own mule.

Benaiah is in the room, but he's not the one David names for this job. The king says, “There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him king over Israel.” Benaiah is told to go along and help with the ram's horn.

Right. David says Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint Solomon king at Gihon. Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, is one of the three men David calls in, and he answers, “Amen.” The anointing isn't his job.
That's what Benaiah says. He asks that the LORD be with Solomon “…and make his throne even greater than that of my lord King David.” He says this to David's face, and he doesn't hold back.
A safe throne would be a fine thing to pray for, baker. But it's not what Benaiah says. He asks that the LORD “…make his throne even greater than that of my lord King David.”
Being known sounds like a good wish, but Benaiah doesn't say it here. His words are about the throne itself. He asks that the LORD “…make his throne even greater than that of my lord King David.”

That's right. Zadok the priest “…took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon.” It was oil taken from the tabernacle. Then they blew the ram's horn, and all the people proclaimed, “Long live King Solomon!”
Water would be a simple thing to grab, but it's not in the text. Zadok the priest “…took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon.” The horn held oil.
Incense smells wonderful, friend, but it's not what's in the horn. The text says Zadok the priest “…took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon.” The anointing is done with oil.

explanations.answer: The earth splits from the sound
explanations.explanation: That's the text. The people follow Solomon “…playing flutes and rejoicing with such a great joy that the earth was split by the sound.” That's one loud celebration.

explanations.answer: The city walls start to shake
explanations.explanation: Shaking walls would be loud, I'll give you that. But the text goes bigger. It says they rejoice “…with such a great joy that the earth was split by the sound.” Walls aren't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: It echoes all the way to Joppa
explanations.explanation: Joppa isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage, baker. The text says the people rejoice “…with such a great joy that the earth was split by the sound.” The sound itself splits the earth.
Not at all, and those are his actual words. Adonijah says, “You must be bringing good news.” Jonathan answers, “Not at all…” and then tells him that David has made Solomon king.
Yep. Adonijah says Jonathan must be bringing good news, but Jonathan replies, “Not at all…” Then he says, “Our lord King David has made Solomon king.” That's not the news Adonijah said he expected.

That's what Jonathan says. “Moreover, Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne.” He's not just anointed, he's sitting on the throne. Jonathan has already told Adonijah that Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed Solomon king at Gihon.
Solomon does ride a mule down to Gihon earlier, but Jonathan doesn't mention Hebron. He says, “…Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne.” He's sitting in the king's seat now.
The tabernacle is where Zadok got the horn of oil. But Jonathan doesn't say Solomon is praying there. He says, “…Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne.”

Yes. Jonathan says the king “…has bowed in worship on his bed…” He tells Adonijah that David is saying, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel!” Then comes the rest of it: “Today He has provided one to sit on my throne, and my eyes have seen it.”

That one is true, baker. Jonathan says David has bowed in worship on his bed. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel! Today He has provided one to sit on my throne, and my eyes have seen it.”

explanations.answer: Rise up in terror and scatter
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The text says all the guests of Adonijah “…arose in terror and scattered.” The party ends fast.
Bowing to Adonijah isn't what they do, friend. After Jonathan's news, the guests “…arose in terror and scattered.” They get up and scatter instead.
Gihon is where Solomon was anointed, but the guests don't go there. The text says they “…arose in terror and scattered.” They head in different directions.

That's right, baker. Adonijah, “…in fear of Solomon, got up and went to take hold of the horns of the altar.” The text names his fear of Solomon outright. I think he grabs the altar because he's afraid, but that part is my guess.
The ark is a holy thing, and it isn't the one in this verse. The text says Adonijah went “…to take hold of the horns of the altar.” That's where he goes.
Adonijah wanted the throne, baker, but he's not holding it. The text says that in fear of Solomon he went “…to take hold of the horns of the altar.” The throne is where Solomon sits.

explanations.answer: Not to put him to the sword
explanations.explanation: That's his request. Adonijah says, “Let King Solomon first swear to me not to put his servant to the sword.” He asks for that oath first. He says it while he has taken hold of the horns of the altar.

explanations.answer: To give him a city of his own
explanations.explanation: A city of his own would be a big ask, friend, and he doesn't make it. Adonijah says, “Let King Solomon first swear to me not to put his servant to the sword.” He's asking for his life.

explanations.answer: To let him keep his chariots
explanations.explanation: Adonijah did acquire chariots earlier, but he's not asking about them here. He says, “Let King Solomon first swear to me not to put his servant to the sword.” What he's asking for is his life.

explanations.answer: Whether he's a man of character
explanations.explanation: That's Solomon's answer. He says, “If he is a man of character, not a single hair of his will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die.” Solomon names two conditions with two outcomes. Whether Adonijah is a man of character or evil is found in him is what he points to.

David is still alive in this scene, but Solomon doesn't mention him. He says, “If he is a man of character, not a single hair of his will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die.” The two outcomes he names rest on character and evil, and nothing in them is about David's forgiveness.

explanations.answer: Whether he leaves Jerusalem for good
explanations.explanation: Leaving the city isn't part of Solomon's answer. He says, “If he is a man of character, not a single hair of his will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die.” It's about Adonijah's character.
That's the order. Solomon says to Adonijah, “Go to your home.” Adonijah has just come down from the altar and bowed down before him. It's the one order Solomon gives him.
Leaving the city would be a harsher order, baker, but Solomon doesn't give it. He says, “Go to your home.” The order is to go home.
Standing guard would put Adonijah right next to the king, friend. That's not what Solomon says. His one order is, “Go to your home.”
